disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a distorted perception of body weight or shape or an undue influence of weight/shape on self-evaluation. It often begins in adolescence or young adulthood but can emerge or recur later in life, and may follow a chronic, relapsing course if untreated. Individuals may deny the seriousness of their low weight and engage in rigid dietary rules, excessive exercise, or other weight-control behaviors, despite medical compromise. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the presence of significantly low body weight and the centrality of weight loss and thinness in the person’s self-concept, even when binge eating or purging are absent.

narrative.stressor: Randall’s eating patterns began to change after a series of cardiac evaluations two years ago, when his primary care physician warned him about elevated cholesterol and suggested weight loss and dietary restrictions to protect his heart. His naturally meticulous, perfectionistic streak—once applied to woodworking and art tours—shifted toward tightly controlling his meals, especially as he watched several close friends from his senior walking club struggle with heart disease and frailty. When his wife had a minor stroke last year, he took on more caregiving responsibilities and quietly doubled down on simplifying meals to "healthy essentials," proud that he could "keep them both on track" even as neighbors and his walking group commented on how thin he had become. The situation came to clinical attention after a routine cardiology follow-up showed further weight loss and concerning lab abnormalities; his cardiologist noted his insistence that the weight was "only good discipline" and referred him for psychiatric evaluation when he continued to restrict food despite medical advice to regain weight.
narrative.chief_complaint: My doctors keep telling me I’m too thin and need to eat more, but I honestly don’t see what the fuss is about—I feel like I’m just being careful with my health.

narrative.stressor: Rebecca’s difficulties intensified during her first year of college, when she moved from her close-knit Pennsylvania town to a larger campus environment where she felt anonymous and academically pressured in her psychology and studio art courses. She threw herself into becoming the "ideal" future art therapist—juggling honors classes, peer-counseling training, and running youth workshops—while quietly comparing herself to classmates and social media influencers who seemed effortlessly composed and slender. Over time, managing her food intake became a way to feel in control amid unpredictable critiques of her artwork, shifting friend groups, and the unpredictability of college life, and she began organizing her days around strict routines that left little room for shared meals or spontaneous outings. Her resident advisor and an art professor eventually noticed her marked weight loss, fatigue, and withdrawal from the Trailblazers Club and encouraged her to see campus health; after being told she was underweight and at risk of needing to withdraw for medical reasons, she reluctantly agreed to a psychiatric evaluation because she was terrified of losing her academic progress and future career plans.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like if I don’t keep really tight control over what I eat, I’ll gain weight and everything I’ve worked for will fall apart.

narrative.stressor: Pedro’s restrictive eating emerged gradually in the months after a difficult separation from his wife, a period when he was adjusting to living alone for the first time and managing increased responsibilities at his sales job. Without the familiar structure of shared meals and family gatherings, he began jogging longer distances and trimming portions under the guise of "getting back in shape" and presenting a more polished image to clients and potential partners. The more chaotic his emotional life felt, the more he leaned on rigid routines around food and exercise, finding a sense of control in tracking every bite and pound, even as his family in Little Havana quietly worried that he looked unwell and no longer enjoyed the traditional dishes he once loved to cook. His supervisor eventually commented on his gaunt appearance and decreased stamina on business trips, and after a faint episode following a morning run, Pedro agreed to see his primary care doctor; when he admitted he was constantly preoccupied with maintaining his lower weight despite already being very thin, he was referred for psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I feel like my whole sense of whether I’m doing okay depends on keeping my body as lean as possible, and it’s starting to take over my life.
